extracted.intended_audience: law students, patent practitioners, and judges
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of doctrines on inventorship (employer/employee contributions, when suggestions defeat a patent, requirement for assignments) and on the extent to which an abstract principle or natural law can be the subject of letters-patent (enablement, claim scope, embodied principle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestions sufficient to enable complete machine
rubrics_metrics.description: The suggestions must have been sufficient to enable C. [the patentee], in this case, to construct a complete and perfect machine. If, after all the suggestions, there was something left for him to devise and work out by his own skill or ingenuity, he is to be regarded as the first and original discoverer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the communications of another go to make up a complete and perfect machine embodying all that is embraced in the patent subsequently issued, the patent is invalid because the real discovery belongs to another. (Pitts v. Hall; Sparkman v. Higgins.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee suggestions not deprive employer unless complete invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a master-workman has conceived the plan of an invention and is engaged in experiments to perfect it, suggestions from a person employed by him are not sufficient to deprive the employer of the exclusive property in the perfected improvement, unless such suggestions amount to a new method or arrangement which in itself is a complete invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case example: Agawam Company v. Jordan — suggestions by Winslow were only auxiliary parts and did not form the entire invention or any separate combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: For suggestions to defeat a patent they must enable an ordinary mechanic
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestions from another, made during experiments, must have embraced the plan of the improvement, and must have furnished such information that it would have enabled an ordinary mechanic, without the exercise of any ingenuity and special skill on his part, to construct and put the improvement in successful operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a test of whether the communicated information itself constituted a complete teaching of the invention (Justice Clifford's formulation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Person who plans the invention is inventor (conception rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The general rule is that the person who plans the invention is to be regarded as the inventor; it will make no difference that such person worked as a servant in the employment of another, provided the servant really conceived the improvement patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the servant truly conceived the invention (not merely executed), he is the inventor — jury question as framed by Baron Alderson; see Minter v. Wells and Arkwright cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of outside scientific advice does not negate inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither can the inquiries he made, or the information or advice he received from men of science, in the course of his researches, impair his right to the character of an inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-level scientific knowledge or assistance necessary to bring a combination invention into practice does not diminish the inventor's rights (O'Reilly v. Morse explanation regarding Morse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention vs mechanical skill (conception vs execution)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Invention is the work of the brain, and not of the hands. If the conception be practically complete, the artist who gives it reflex and embodiment in a machine is no more the inventor than the tools with which he wrought. Mere mechanical skill can never rise to the sphere of invention."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where conception is complete, the mechanic or draughtsman who merely embodies the design is not the inventor (Blandy v. Griffith; Justice Swayne's instruction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordinate/workman improvements belong to original inventor when accessory
rubrics_metrics.description: After the main principle has been discovered, the suggestion by a workman of subordinate improvements accessory to the main principle and tending to carry it out more conveniently may be adopted by the patentee and embodied in his specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the improvement is merely a more convenient mode of carrying out the patentee's principle (not a distinct invention), it is the property of the inventor of the original improved principle (Shaw/cloth-felting machine example; Allen v. Rawson affirmation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for assignment/contract when real author is not patentee
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the relation between parties amounts to a contract by which one agrees to employ his inventive faculties in the service of another, and the workman in the course of employment makes a substantive invention, the question arises whether the employer can become the patentee of that invention without a written assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By the statutes (act of 1836, act of 1837) the right to the patent vests in the inventor and an assignee must have an assignment recorded; courts treat the necessity of some contract or assignment to operate as an assignment prior to issuance as important (Dixon v. Moyer discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of a claim attempting to patent a principle (Morse)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that purports to cover the essence of an invention (e.g., 'the use of the motive-power of the electric or galvanic current ... however developed, for marking or printing intelligible characters') without limitation as to means may be invalid for being unlimited in respect to the means by which the principle could be effected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In O'Reilly v. Morse a majority held such a broad claim invalid; the question is whether the inventor can monopolize the application of a natural force by any and all machinery or only his specific machinery and equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: A mere elementary principle is not patentable unless embodied
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere elementary principle cannot be made the subject of a patent; but a principle so far embodied and connected with corporeal substances as to be in a condition to act and to produce effects in any art, trade, mystery, or manual occupation, may be patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lord Chief Justice Eyre's formulation in Boulton & Watt: the patentee must describe a practical manner of doing it — i.e., the application must be embodied in means (Watt's separate condenser discussion; Hartley's fire-proofing method example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of a law/truth of nature not itself a manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery of a law, or truth, or fact in nature is not of itself a manufacture and thus not patentable in the abstract; but the new application of a force of nature or property of matter by described mechanical means may constitute patentable subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction is central to analyses of patents claiming principles or natural laws (discussion contrasting Watt and Morse issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must enable a mechanic to construct the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must describe the invention sufficiently to enable mechanics acquainted with the art to build and put it in operation according to the inventor's plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Watt's case a special verdict found the specification sufficient to enable a mechanic to build an engine operating on the plan; enablement affects whether the patent is for a manufacture and the permissible scope of claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent must point out the improvement, not overclaim prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patentee claims the whole of an old engine without pointing out his own improvement in the mechanism, the patent may be void for overclaiming; the patentee must describe the improvement he relies on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice Buller's concern in the Watt litigation: patents cannot be construed to monopolize the entire prior art rather than the new improvement.
